Defect type: Duplicate transaction by business key (distinct id, identical content)
Severity rationale: Two postings on the same account, same date, same type, same operation, same amount and the same resulting balance are the same event recorded twice: a genuinely distinct second posting would have moved the balance. The primary key cannot catch this, which is exactly why the rule exists. It double counts flows in Q5 and breaks the balance chain behind Q9. One instance fires on this copy of the data.
Handling: Keep the lowest trans_id, quarantine the rest with the reason naming the surviving row, so the decision is auditable rather than implicit.
Example: identical to trans_id 3456218 (account 9051, 1998-02-28, amount 0.00, balance 1367.10); group size 2

Defect type: Account has several postings on its latest date (closing posting must be derived)
Severity rationale: trans_id is not chronological within a date and the source has no time of day, so when an account has several postings on one day the closing one has to be derived. 183 accounts have this on their most recent date, which is the balance Q9 reports. The running balance resolves it (D028): each posting starts at balance_after - signed_amount, and the closing posting is the end of that chain. That settles 141 of the 183; for the other 42 the chain does not order the postings, the documented fallback is used and the month-end row is marked closing_basis = 'ambiguous'. Warn: the data is not wrong, the order has to be inferred.
Handling: Closing posting taken from the running-balance chain in core.fact_account_month_end_balance (closing_basis records how); accounts flagged so the caveat can be quantified.
Example: account has 2 postings on its latest date 1998-12-31; the closing posting is derived from the running-balance chain

Severity rationale: 114 owners were under 15 when their account was opened, the youngest 10.3 years. A ten year old cannot be the legal holder of a current account, so either the birth number or the owner flag is wrong. It is warn rather than block because the accounts and their transactions are otherwise well-formed and feed Q5, Q6 and Q9 correctly: quarantining 114 accounts to protect the age metric would damage four answers to improve one. Q7 and Q8 report their coverage instead. | 6 loans were granted to owners recorded as under 15. Q7 reports exactly this number -- the average age of the owner at loan start, per status -- so these rows pull the answer directly. Warn rather than block because the loan amount and status are themselves sound and feed Q2, Q3, Q4 and Q10: removing the loans would make the certified loan total disagree with the source. Q7 publishes the flagged count next to the average, which is the honest treatment of a value that is probably wrong but not certainly so.
Handling: Rows kept and flagged (_dq_flags carries 'owner_age_implausible'); the semantic layer attaches the caveat to the age metric so the LLM can repeat it. | Rows kept and flagged; Q7 reports the average with and without the flagged loans so the sensitivity is visible.
Example: owner was 11.9 years old when account 9 was opened

Severity rationale: Tested order independently: the sum of all signed amounts on an account should equal its last reported balance, whatever order the postings are read in. The last reported balance is the end of the last day's running-balance chain (D028). 84 accounts breach a 1 CZK tolerance; 70 of those are within 100 CZK and sit in the rounding band (every amount in the source carries a single decimal, so residuals accumulate). The earlier highest-trans_id choice of "last balance" made 136 accounts appear to breach, 52 of them only because it read a mid-day balance. Warn, because the account is still usable and the Q9 average moves by cents; the band is reported so nobody confuses it with the material tier below. | 14 accounts are off by more than 100 CZK (largest 488.30 CZK, account 8856), which is a missing or extra posting rather than rounding. Before D028 the rule read a mid-day balance as the last one and reported 55, including an apparent 1,200 CZK break that was not real. This is the single most material finding for Q9, because the answer is an average balance and these accounts' balances cannot be derived from their own flows. It stays warn rather than block on purpose: the balance column is what Q9 reads, and it is internally plausible -- it is the *flows* that disagree with it. Quarantining the accounts would remove real balances from an average; blocking the postings would break the chain further. The defensible treatment is to publish the answer with the affected population and the residual attached, which is what the semantic layer makes the LLM do.
Handling: Account flagged; the month-end balance fact carries the residual so a user can see the size of the discrepancy next to the balance. | Account flagged as balance_unreconciled; Q9 reports the average together with the number of affected accounts and the total residual, so the reader can size the uncertainty instead of guessing at it.

Defect type: Counterparty missing on a transfer posting
Severity rationale: This is the non-structural half of the rule above: a remittance or collection (PREVOD NA UCET / PREVOD Z UCTU) with no counterparty is a genuine gap, because a transfer by definition has another side. No certified metric reads it today, but it is evidence of a broken feed rather than a design choice, so it is warn and not info.
Handling: Row kept and flagged; counted separately from the structural NULLs.
Example: transfer posting without counterparty; operation = PREVOD NA UCET

Defect type: Missing values in columns no certified metric reads
Severity rationale: No answer to the 10 questions reads this column, so a null here cannot change a reported number. It is logged with its null rate so that the next metric built on this column starts from a known baseline, and it is promoted to warn or block the moment a metric does read it.
Handling: Normalised to a real NULL in stg (placeholders '?', '', 'NA' and a bare space all collapse), original text preserved in the matching *_raw audit column, null rate published in dq/results/profile.md.

Defect type: Counterparty bank and account absent for non-transfer postings
Severity rationale: 760,931 postings have neither partner bank nor partner account. These are cash operations and bank-generated postings, which have no counterparty by construction. No question reads the counterparty. Reported as info with the cross-check that it never happens on a transfer operation, which is the version of this that *would* be a defect.
Handling: Left as NULL by design; documented as structural in the semantic layer.
Example: partner_bank and partner_account are both NULL; operation = NULL

Defect type: The same column encodes 'missing' three different ways in the source
Severity rationale: In raw.trans.k_symbol, "no category" arrives as a quoted empty string (481,871 rows), as an unquoted empty field that loads as NULL (10 rows) and as a single space. The three spellings mean one thing. No answer changes because stg collapses them, but it is reported because any consumer reading raw directly -- including an LLM pointed at the wrong layer -- would have to know about all three to filter correctly. That is exactly the kind of knowledge a semantic layer exists to remove.
Handling: Collapsed to a single NULL by stg.norm_text; the raw spelling is kept in k_symbol_raw. Rule runs against raw, so it keeps reporting even after stg is clean.

Defect type: Transaction operation absent (structurally, for interest postings)
Severity rationale: 183,114 postings have no operation. Every one of them is an interest credit (k_symbol = UROK): the bank's own interest run has no customer operation behind it, so the NULL means "not applicable" rather than "unknown". None of the 10 questions groups by operation. It is reported as info precisely so that nobody later imputes a value into it, which would invent an operation that never happened.
Handling: Left as NULL by design, labelled 'not applicable (bank-generated posting)' in the semantic layer so an LLM does not treat it as missing.

Defect type: Balance after the transaction is negative (overdraft)
Severity rationale: 2,999 postings leave a negative balance. This is overdraft, which is normal banking, not a defect -- and it matters that the rule says so, because the tempting "fix" (clipping balances at zero) would bias the Q9 average upwards. Reported as info so the number is known and explicitly not acted on.
Handling: Logged only; balances are never clipped.

Defect type: Owner's own district differs from the district of the account they own
Severity rationale: 409 of 4,500 owners (9.1 percent) live in a different district than their account is registered in. This is not a defect: people move, and they bank where they opened the account. It is reported as info with an interpretation because it is a modelling fork, not a data error -- Q1 (clients per region) and Q5 (districts by transaction volume) would give different answers depending on which district is used, so both questions state their choice, and the 9.1 percent figure is what tells a reviewer the choice is material.
Handling: Logged with its rate. Q1 uses the client's own district, Q5 uses the account's district; both are stated in the semantic layer and in ASSUMPTIONS so an LLM cannot pick silently.
Example: client 12 lives in district 40 but owns account 9 in district 70

Defect type: Two clients share birth number and district (possible duplicate person)
Severity rationale: A repeated birth number within one district is a candidate duplicate person, which would inflate Q1 and Q8. It is info rather than warn because the birth number only encodes date of birth and sex, so collisions are expected in a 5,369 client book and most of them are genuinely different people. It is reported so that a real master-data process can pick it up, and so that nobody mistakes the collision rate for a defect rate.
Handling: Logged only; no row is changed or removed.

Defect type: Transaction amount is zero or negative
Severity rationale: 14 postings have an amount of exactly zero. All of them are interest or sanction-interest runs that accrued nothing, so they are genuine events with no monetary effect: they change no sum in Q5 and no balance in Q9. The naive form of this rule ("amount must be > 0") would quarantine 14 valid postings and break the balance chain of 14 accounts, which is a worked example of a defensible rule with the wrong severity doing more damage than the defect. A *negative* amount, by contrast, would be blocked: the split is in the rule below.
Handling: Logged only; the postings stay in core with amount = 0.

Defect type: Placeholder '?' in the 1995 unemployment and crime columns
Severity rationale: One district (69, Jesenik) carries '?' instead of a number in unemployment_rate_1995 and crimes_1995. None of the 10 questions reads either column, so no reported number changes. It is info *today* and becomes warn the moment a metric uses the 1995 series, because an average over 76 of 77 districts silently answers a different question than the one asked. The rule stays in place to make that promotion a one-line change.
Handling: '?' normalised to NULL in stg, original text kept in unemployment_rate_1995_raw / crimes_1995_raw, district row otherwise used normally.
